title: Is the four-day week worth it?

turns.speaker: Hannah
turns.text: So my company finished its four-day week trial last month, and they're keeping it. Same pay, Fridays off.

turns.speaker: Marcus
turns.text: Same pay? Okay, that surprises me. How did anyone sell that upstairs?

turns.speaker: Hannah
turns.text: Output didn't drop. That was the whole argument, really. They tracked it for six months and it came out more or less flat, and sick days fell by about a third.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Flat output while everybody knows they're being measured, though. That's not nothing, but it isn't proof either. People try harder when they're being watched.

turns.speaker: Hannah
turns.text: Sure, but six months is a long time to keep that up.

turns.speaker: Marcus
turns.text: What I want to know is what actually changed in the week. Because if it's the same work squashed into four days, that's not a shorter week, that's a longer day with better marketing.

turns.speaker: Hannah
turns.text: Meetings, mostly. We killed about half of them. Turns out a lot of what we were doing was updating each other about updating each other.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Right, and that's the bit I'd believe.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: But it only works if your job is that kind of job. My sister's a nurse. You can't take a third off her ward and tell her to run fewer meetings.

turns.speaker: Marcus
turns.text: That's fair. It probably does land differently depending on the sector.

turns.speaker: Hannah
turns.text: Nobody's claiming it works everywhere. The point is it works somewhere, and most offices assumed it worked nowhere.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: I'd just want to see it after three years, when the novelty's gone and nobody's writing a report about it.

points: Hannah's company kept the four-day week after a six-month trial, on the same pay, because measured output stayed roughly flat and sick days fell by about a third.
Priya questions the evidence: people work harder while they know they are being measured, so flat output during a trial is not proof.
Marcus's test is whether the work itself changed, or whether the same work was simply compressed into longer days.
Hannah says the saving came mostly from cutting about half the meetings.
Priya argues it only transfers to certain jobs, using nursing as a case where staffing cannot simply be reduced.
They end unresolved, with Priya wanting evidence from three years in, once the novelty and the scrutiny have gone.
